title: Transient laws of non-stationary queueing systems and their applications
contribution: A transient Little's law and transient distributional laws for overtake-free non-stationary single- and multiclass queues, used to write complete integral-equation descriptions of six system types that are then solved by exact formulae, a recursive algorithm or heavy-traffic asymptotics checked numerically.
problem_entry: SD: transient analysis 'has long been considered a very difficult problem', yet non-stationary models are needed and steady state is reached too slowly (pp. 1-2); question: are there transient laws linking L(t) and S(t), and how can they be used (p. 2); entry by structural relations instead of simulation or numerics, building on Little's law and the Haji-Newell distributional laws (p. 2).
key_idea: Transient Little's law E[L(t)] = integral of h(u)P{S(u) > t-u} du plus an initial-customer term (Theorems 1-2, pp. 6-7) and transient distributional laws for overtake-free systems (Theorems 6-7, pp. 12-14); for each system the laws give as many integral equations as unknowns, which are then solved by the fitting technique (p. 3; table p. 19).
assumptions: A.1 conditionally independent interarrivals (renewal, nonhomogeneous Poisson), A.2 FIFO exits ('the crucial assumption'), A.3 no blocking, balking or reneging, A.4 independent class streams (pp. 5, 9); stationary service requirements with a time-varying service rate (p. 5); initial work served first without idling (Assumptions B, C, pp. 7, 21); heavy traffic rho -> 1 with t -> infinity (p. 28).
proof_devices: Sample-path count as an integral of indicators plus Fubini for the transient Little's law; initial customers as an additive term (Theorems 1-2, pp. 6-8)
Event {L(t) >= n} = the nth most recent arrival is still present, split into an arrival at u, n-1 later arrivals and a sojourn above t-u, independent by A.1 (pp. 12-13)
Non-overtake-free M(t)/GI(t)/infinity handled by deterministic-service classes (thinned Poisson streams) and limits of mixtures (Theorem 10, pp. 20-21)
Single-server systems reduced to the emptiness function idle(t) (Proposition 11, Theorem 12, pp. 22-23)
Heavy-traffic kernel expansions as z -> 1 and s, w -> 0 (Proposition 15, p. 28) and an analyticity argument for the double transform (appendix, pp. 39-40)
experiments: Kernel expansion checked against Laplace inversion by two algorithms (Hosono; Abate-Whitt) programmed in Matlab that agreed exactly; exact for t > 20, best near Poisson arrivals (p. 29); idle(t) and E[Q]-E[Q(t)] against Brownian approximations and Odoni-Roth exact values, agreement only after t0 of about 12-80 depending on variability, t < 15 withheld (p. 34); M(t)/GI(t)/1 numbers omitted as identical to Choudhury et al. (p. 25); a comparison with simulation is promised in the introduction (p. 3) but no simulation runs appear in the text; no run times.
positioning: A 'different standpoint' from simulation, approximate numerics (Odoni-Roth, Malone, Ong-Taaffe) and exact numerics (Choudhury et al.; Green-Kolesar-Svoronos) (p. 2); Theorem 10 credited to pre-1958 authors and Massey-Whitt (p. 21); Choudhury et al. reached the M(t)/G(t)/1 recursion independently (p. 25).
writing: Numbered contributions and a results table by system (pp. 2-3, 19); applications framed as demonstrating 'the power' of the laws (pp. 1, 3, 38); the reviewer thanked for substantial improvements (p. 38).
limits_future: Overtake-free systems only (p. 9); multiclass law with arbitrary initial conditions omitted as complicated (p. 19); GI/GI/1 integral equation hard to solve analytically (p. 26); Corollary 18 only asymptotic in heavy traffic (p. 34); future: queueing laws for multiserver systems and networks, 'the major open problem' (p. 38).

method_links.note: Formulation first, but as a complete set of laws giving enough integral equations for the unknowns of each system, not a class-kept LP, conic or MIO model; boundary printed (overtake-free only; multiserver systems and networks open). No optimization in the paper: evidence for the probability side of Tension T3.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 10 recovers the pre-1958 Poisson result for M(t)/G/infinity; the heavy-traffic analysis recovers the authors' steady-state E[Q] and E[W]; the M(t)/GI(t)/1 recursion matches Choudhury et al.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The steady-state distributional laws of Bertsimas-Mourtzinou [4, 5] and the stationary Little's law are made transient, with initial conditions explicit.

transferable: Prove a time-t version of a steady-state law by writing the sample-path count as an integral of indicators and exchanging expectation and integral; initial customers become an additive term (pp. 6-8).
In a FIFO system, derive distributional relations from the event that the nth most recent arrival is still present, split into arrival time, later arrivals and sojourn tail (pp. 12-13).
Extend a deterministic-service result to general service by treating each service value as a thinned Poisson class and passing to mixtures (pp. 20-21).
Validate an asymptotic expansion against numerical inversion by two independent algorithms that must agree, and report the time after which it holds (pp. 29, 34).

quotes.text: This paper takes a different standpoint, trying to identify structural relationships between the fundamental quantities of queueing systems that evolve over time.
The major open problem is to identify queueing laws for these systems.

title: Estimation of time-varying parameters in statistical models: an optimization approach
contribution: Nonparametric regression under a Lipschitz assumption written as one convex QP (least squares with pairwise Lipschitz constraints) with a max-of-cones extension, plus a Lipschitz-constrained maximum-likelihood variant (DMLE), proven average-unbiased and uniformly, almost surely consistent with exponential tails, and compared with kernel regression on synthetic data (read in its Machine Learning 35, 1999 journal version).
problem_entry: ML (CP as the engine): nonlinear regression Y = f(X) + noise, with the time-varying mean as the motivating case (p. 1); parametric forms are assumed, kernel regression and smoothing splines are the nonparametric standard; what can convex optimization do when f is only Lipschitz (p. 2). Text read: the Machine Learning 35 (1999) journal version, not the COLT 1997 paper.
key_idea: Minimize squared errors subject to |f_i - f_j| <= K||X_i - X_j||_inf (QP (2)) and extend by f(x) = max_i{f_i - K||x - X_i||}, which keeps K (Proposition 1, pp. 3-4); consecutive constraints suffice in time (p. 4); the same constraints give DMLE, concave for Bernoulli and exponential, nonconvex for Gaussian with unknown sigma (pp. 6-9); smoothness as a hard constraint instead of a spline penalty, with an exact fit when the noise is zero (pp. 2, 5).
assumptions: Conditionally zero-mean independent noise (p. 3); Lipschitz in the max norm with unknown K0, K guessed, K >= K0 sufficient (pp. 3, 5); Theorem 2 adds X in [0,1]^d, Y in [0,1] and a density floor beta > 0, which excludes Gaussian noise and Example 4.1 (pp. 12-13); synthetic data only, Y = sin X + N(0, sigma^2) on a grid of [0, 2pi] (pp. 9-10).
proof_devices: Average unbiasedness: shifting all fitted values by a constant keeps feasibility, so optimality in the constant forces the residuals to sum to zero (Theorem 1, pp. 5-6)
Max-of-cones extension preserving the Lipschitz constant and interpolating the fitted values (Proposition 1, pp. 3-4)
Estimator as empirical risk minimization over the Lipschitz class with the Lee-Bartlett-Williamson uniform deviation bound (Proposition 2, pp. 14-15)
Kolmogorov-Tihomirov covering-number bound independent of n, log VC entropy O((K/eps)^d) (Proposition 3, pp. 15, 19-20)
L2 tail bounds, then an L2-to-sup-norm lemma for Lipschitz functions under a density floor, then Borel-Cantelli (Propositions 4-5, Lemma 1, pp. 16-17)
Tractability asserted, not measured: convex QP with linear constraints, polynomial by interior-point methods (p. 5)
experiments: Y = sin X, n = 100, sigma from 0.5 to 0.001; K in {1, 2} against Gaussian-kernel regression with delta in {0.3, 0.1}; d_inf and d2 errors (Tables 1-2, pp. 10-11); insensitive to K, best K slightly below K0 = 1 (Fig. 2, n = 50, pp. 11-12); kernel ties or wins at some (sigma, delta), the QP wins as noise shrinks (p. 12); sample-size curve over 40 repetitions (p. 12); no solver, run time or constraint count; slips: Fig. 1 caption K = 1 against text K = 2 (p. 10), and the text calls Table 2's errors larger though Table 1 holds the larger values (p. 11).
positioning: Uniform a.s. consistency known for kernel regression (Devroye 1978) but, to the authors' knowledge, not for smoothing splines (p. 2); concedes kernel regression's optimal O(n^-2/3) rate, unproven for this method (p. 18); proof machinery from statistical learning theory (Vapnik, Haussler, Lee-Bartlett-Williamson) (pp. 14-15); cited in 2025 by S317 as early slowly varying regression (S317 p. 5).
writing: Three-item contribution list with section pointers (p. 2); impractical constants admitted in the introduction and repeated (pp. 2, 13, 17); remark lists after each algorithm (pp. 5, 7, 13).
limits_future: Constants 'too large for practical purposes, even for dimension d = 1' (p. 17); samples exponential in d, 'unavoidable' (p. 13); rate unproven, O(n^-2/5) from the bounds against a simulated O(n^-2/3) (p. 18); the choice of K crucial and open (p. 19); future: DMLE consistency, expected-error bounds, setting K, a kernel plus Lipschitz-constraint hybrid, and a varying-coefficient model b(t)'z with log VC entropy O(d) (pp. 17-19).

method_links.note: A problem owned by nonparametric statistics written exactly as a convex QP, the class named (convex objective, linear constraints, polynomial-time interior-point methods) and the boundary printed (Gaussian with unknown variance nonconvex; samples exponential in d); 1997-1999, before the CRIO line.

One interpretable knob K indexes the estimators, with a guarantee condition K >= K0 and an error-against-K curve, but the knob is a smoothness bound, not a property priced for a decision-maker, and how to set it is left open.

Duel against the incumbent (kernel regression at two bandwidths) on synthetic data with known truth, saying where the incumbent ties or wins; no warm start or certificate is needed because the QP is solved exactly, and no solve time is reported.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The constants of the tail bound are admitted to be practically useless; the proven O(n^-2/5) rate is set against the simulated O(n^-2/3), suggested as the true rate.

transferable: Turn a qualitative shape assumption into pairwise linear constraints on fitted values and extend off-sample with f(x) = max_i{f_i - K||x - X_i||}, which keeps the constant (pp. 3-4).
Prove average unbiasedness by shift invariance: if adding a constant keeps feasibility, optimality in that constant makes the residuals sum to zero (pp. 5-6).

Prove consistency of a constrained least-squares estimator by ERM over the class, an n-free covering-number bound, and an L2-to-sup-norm step via the Lipschitz constant and a density floor (pp. 14-17).
For maximum likelihood with smoothly varying parameters, check concavity family by family before claiming tractability (pp. 7-9).

quotes.text: The resulting optimization problem has a convex objective function and linear constraints, and as a result, is efficiently solvable.
the constants in our estimates of the tail probabilities are too large to be practically useful.

title: The parsimonious property of cut covering problems and its applications
contribution: Characterizes the set functions (symmetric, node-subadditive and quasi-supermodular, or the weaker Conditions C) for which degree constraints leave the LP relaxation of cutset covering problems unchanged, proves it by LP duality, and uses it for short integrality proofs, a new proof and algorithm for the 2(1 - 1/|T|) bound, and a unified view of edge-disjoint-path results.
problem_entry: IO (LO as the engine): cutset IPs with a set function f and degree constraints model Steiner tree, TSP, VRP, matching, T-join and survivable network design (pp. 1, 4); the entry is the Goemans-Bertsimas parsimonious property for survivable networks (Theorem 1, p. 2); goal: the class of f for which it holds and its implications (p. 2).
key_idea: Conditions B (symmetry, node subadditivity, quasi-supermodularity) generalize proper functions and cover b-matching and the capacitated-tree VRP relaxation (pp. 2-3); Theorem 2: under the triangle inequality Z_f(D) = Z_f(empty set) for all D (p. 4); used for non-algorithmic integrality proofs (Theorems 5-7, p. 6), a new proof and algorithm for 2(1 - 1/|T|) (Theorem 8, pp. 7-8), and weaker Conditions C unifying edge-disjoint-path results (pp. 8-10).
assumptions: Undirected graph with nonnegative costs (p. 1); the triangle inequality, free when D is empty via the shortest-path metric closure (Theorem 4, p. 5); integral costs for Theorem 8 without loss (p. 7); 0-1 proper f for the approximation result (p. 7).
proof_devices: LP duality: uncross the dual support into a laminar family (QS), complement the sets containing v, shift Delta among y(v), y(A + v) and y(A); feasibility by the triangle inequality, optimality by symmetry and node subadditivity (pp. 4-5)
Two small counterexamples with an empty polyhedron show both conditions are necessary (p. 5)
Metric closure: reroute flow along shortest paths so costs satisfy the triangle inequality without changing values (Theorem 4, p. 5)

Sandwich integrality proofs through a known integral polytope (T-join from perfect matching; Steiner 2-connected via the subtour polytope on at most 5 nodes; single-source multicommodity flow) (Theorems 5-7, p. 6)
Minimal counterexample (fewest nodes, then least total cost) with a dual-feasibility contradiction (Theorem 8, p. 7)
Lovasz splitting-off for weakly parsimonious functions (Theorem 9, pp. 8-9)
positioning: Generalizes Goemans-Bertsimas and Goemans-Williamson (pp. 2-3); the proof extends Frank's observation for matching (pp. 2, 4); Goemans's independent unpublished generalization acknowledged twice (pp. 2, 10); the algorithm compared with Goemans-Williamson's reverse deletion (pp. 7-8); edge-disjoint-path theorems of Rothschild-Whinston, Seymour and Lomonosov re-derived (p. 9).
writing: Four numbered contributions (p. 2); 'interesting and indeed surprising' (p. 4) and 'genuinely simple proofs' (p. 6); a tedious case analysis omitted as off-theme (p. 10); no conclusion section (p. 10).
limits_future: Triangle inequality required; repeated shortest-path computations because reduced costs may violate it (footnote, p. 8); edge-disjoint-path proof incomplete in print (p. 10); arbitrary proper f only within 2W(p1, ..., pn) (p. 8); no future work stated.

method_links.note: LP duality as the proof device; structure read off a chosen optimal dual (laminar support, nonnegative degree duals); boundary printed by counterexamples.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The LP relaxation is the object (its value is invariant to degree constraints), the tool (integrality proofs) and the yardstick (IP/LP ratio); with S052 (card c02) and S166 (this batch).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: T-join integrality from the perfect-matching polytope; the MST heuristic's Steiner-tree bound as a case of Theorem 8; edge-disjoint-path theorems unified by the 2-QS property.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: own earlier result's limit as the entry
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The 1993 Goemans-Bertsimas survivable-network theorem generalized to a class of set functions.

transferable: To show extra constraints leave an LP value unchanged, choose a structured optimal dual (uncrossed, laminar) and move dual weight off the extra constraints while keeping feasibility and the objective (pp. 4-5).
Get the triangle inequality for free by metric closure and rerouting along shortest paths (Theorem 4, p. 5).
Prove integrality by sandwiching IP and LP values between a known integral polytope and the structural property (Theorems 5-7, p. 6).
Prove an approximation ratio by a minimal counterexample: drop zero-demand vertices, contract zero-cost edges, lower all costs by a uniform dual step (p. 7).
Show each hypothesis is necessary with a 3- or 4-node counterexample (p. 5).

quotes.text: It is thus interesting and indeed surprising that the parsimonious property holds for the LP relaxations of these problems.
At first sight these results appear to be unrelated without a unifying characteristic.

title: Pricing and hedging derivative securities in incomplete markets: an ε-arbitrage approach
contribution: NBER working-paper version (w6250) of the epsilon-arbitrage paper S069: mean-squared optimal replication by stochastic DP, plus a Section 3 later dropped from the journal version, in which the same loss under the equivalent martingale measure makes the minimum production cost the equilibrium price and yields generalized delta hedging.
problem_entry: AP+SD: same entry as S069 (dynamic spanning fails under frictions, closures and discrete trading; how close can replication come?) (pp. 5-6), but 'Pricing' leads the title and a pricing result is claimed (pp. 1, 6-7).
key_idea: Shared with S069: quadratic value function and linear policy by stochastic DP (Theorems 1-2, pp. 15-18) and epsilon* as the degree of incompleteness (p. 6). Working paper only: the loss under the equivalent martingale measure gives the equilibrium price (Theorem 3, p. 22); generalized delta hedging, reducing to Black-Scholes-Merton when the state variables are uncorrelated (pp. 23-25); routes to the measure, theoretical and empirical (pp. 23-26); risk-neutral stochastic-volatility numbers (section 5.5, pp. 48-49).
assumptions: (A1)-(A4): frictionless, zero riskless rate, Markov state not perfectly correlated with traded prices, fixed trading times (p. 10); MSE for tractability, symmetry and, in this version, the risk-neutral interpretation called 'perhaps the most compelling' (pp. 20-21); unconstrained holdings because nonnegativity would be intractable (p. 11); put with strike 1, six months, 25 periods, GBM mu = 0.07, sigma = 0.13, +/-25% and +/-50% variations (p. 37).
proof_devices: Backward induction with first-order conditions; convexity from the positivity of a_i (Theorem 1, pp. 15-16, 59)
Theorem 3 in four lines from the zero-mean optimal error under the martingale measure (Schweizer) and self-financing (p. 22)
Risk-neutral PDE system following Schweizer's (4.4), derived under different assumptions (footnote 19, p. 24)
Proofs sketched, a detailed appendix offered on request (p. 59)
experiments: Against Black-Scholes delta hedging: two illustrative paths (Table 1, pp. 7-8) and 250,000 paths, average error $241.2 against $248.0 (p. 8); grid with piecewise-quadratic interpolation and Gauss-Hermite quadrature, no grid size or run time (p. 36); epsilon* falls from 0.0086 to 0.0060 toward GBM (p. 48); risk-neutral stochastic volatility: replication cost equals the price when volatility risk is unpriced, differs otherwise (pp. 48-49); Table 3, three calibrated models, epsilon* at P0 = 1.00 of 0.0060 (GBM), 0.0068 (jump-diffusion), 0.0084 (stochastic volatility), the order can reverse (pp. 55-56).
positioning: Claims to extend Schweizer by working under the equivalent martingale measure, while conceding it is a special case of his approach made sharper by the Markov assumption (p. 7); the literature on estimating the risk-neutral measure (Ait-Sahalia-Lo, Rubinstein, Longstaff, Jarrow-Rudd and others) is the route to it (p. 25).
writing: 'Pricing' in the title and a 'More importantly' pricing paragraph in the conclusion (p. 57); 'no claims of generality' (p. 58). The journal version (S069) drops 'Pricing', Section 3, section 5.5 and that paragraph, keeping one caveated paragraph (S069 pp. 1, 8, 21).
limits_future: Obtaining the martingale measure is 'the most difficult aspect' (p. 57) and implementing an estimated one is left to future research (p. 26); symmetric loss and unconstrained holdings (pp. 11, 20); proofs sketched (p. 59); the journal version adds that equivalent martingale measures are not unique and that bounds over them are 'likely to be extremely wide' (S069 p. 8).

method_links.note: As in S069: the finance problem kept in a quadratic DP class with exact recursions; boundary printed (nonnegativity constraints would make it intractable); not LP, conic or MIO.
Simulated: hedges scored by replication error against the practitioner's rule (Black-Scholes delta hedging), including a path where the method loses and averages over 250,000 paths.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: epsilon* as the degree of market incompleteness; recurs from S069 and S080 (card c06).

transferable: Change the measure inside a quadratic loss (physical to risk-neutral) to turn a cost-minimizing hedge into a price under stated conditions, then say how the measure would be obtained theoretically and empirically (pp. 21-26).

Before a 'more importantly' claim goes into the abstract or conclusion, check whether it rests on an object that is not unique (here the martingale measure in an incomplete market); the journal version keeps the idea only with that caveat (pp. 21-23, 57; S069 p. 8).

quotes.text: Optimizing this loss function yields a minimum production cost that must equal the equilibrium price of the option

More importantly, we show that if the mean-squared loss function is evaluated with respect to the equivalent martingale measure, the minimum production cost associated with the optimal-replication strategy is the equilibrium price of the derivative security.

title: Asymptotic buffer overflow probabilities in multiclass multiplexers: An optimal control approach
contribution: Tight large-deviations asymptotics of per-class buffer overflow under GPS and a new GLQF policy in a two-class multiplexer with stochastic capacity, obtained by computing the exponent as the value of a deterministic optimal control problem whose optimal paths are the most likely overflow modes, with GLQF proved to dominate GPS (read in the Boston University technical-report version).
problem_entry: SD+AP (communication networks): QoS needs loss probabilities of order 10^-9 (p. 3); exact multiclass G/G/1 network distributions with correlated arrivals are out of reach, so a two-class multiplexer with dedicated buffers and stochastic capacity keeps the salient features (pp. 3-4, 9); question: the large-buffer overflow tail per class under GPS and GLQF (pp. 2-3). Text read: BU report MNS-97-107.
key_idea: Each overflow scenario has probability about exp(-U theta(omega)); the tightest lower bound is a deterministic optimal control problem (scaled queue levels as states, empirical rates as controls, integrated rate functions as cost, free horizon), matched by a sample-path upper bound to first degree in the exponent (pp. 2, 12, 16-18); policies enter only through the dynamics (pp. 5, 46); optimal paths are the two most likely overflow modes (pp. 24-25); policies compared by vectors of class exponents with strict priorities as extreme points (pp. 40-41).
assumptions: Slotted-time fluid model; stationary, mutually independent arrival and service processes with dependence over time (pp. 9-10); stability E[B] > E[A1] + E[A2] (p. 9); Assumptions A (Gartner-Ellis), B (sample-path lower bound) and C ('convex dual analog'), stated to hold for renewal, Markov-modulated and mixing processes (p. 8); two streams only, N streams give exponentially many modes (p. 4).
proof_devices: Lower bound by the most likely scenario, formulated as the optimal control problem (OVERFLOW), motivated heuristically with rigour from the sample-path LDP (pp. 12, 16-18)
Lemma 5.1: Jensen and convexity of the rate functions make controls constant within each dynamics region (pp. 18-19)
Homogeneity: scaled optimal trajectories stay optimal, reducing candidates to a few piecewise-linear shapes (pp. 19-24)
Finite-dimensional exponent formulas (Theorem 9.1, pp. 34-35); strict priority as phi1 in {0, 1} (p. 35)
GPS upper bound deferred to [BPT97b] as 'quite involved'; GLQF upper bound via the largest root of a convex function, independent of the control formulation (p. 26)
Dominance of GLQF over GPS for all admissible inputs by case analysis on the overflow modes (Theorem 10.5, pp. 44-46)
experiments: Figure 6: exponent pairs of GPS(phi1) and GLQF(theta) for Bernoulli inputs A1 ~ Ber(0.3), A2 ~ Ber(0.2), B ~ Ber(0.9), computed with the formulas of Theorems 9.3 and 9.6 (pp. 41-42); the plotted dominance is then proved in general (p. 44); no simulation of overflow, no tool or run time.
positioning: Extends de Veciana-Kesidis and Zhang (deterministic-capacity GPS via G/D/1 departures) to stochastic capacity (pp. 4-5); a control formulation unlike Courcoubetis-Weber's, which needs Lipschitz controls (pp. 4-5); generalizes Gail et al.'s deterministic LQF to GLQF with traffic statistics (p. 4); a worst-case design as in Parekh-Gallager forgoes multiplexing gain (p. 25).
writing: Four contribution bullets (p. 5); heuristic motivation flagged, rigour in a footnote (p. 17); the recommendation hedged 'at least in the absence of fairness considerations' and for delay-insensitive traffic (pp. 5, 41); a long proof deferred to a companion report (pp. 6, 26).
limits_future: Two streams only (pp. 4, 46); log-scale asymptotics to first degree in the exponent (p. 2); GPS upper-bound proof elsewhere (p. 26); fairness and delay not modelled (p. 41); future: N streams (p. 46), admission control in [Pas97] (p. 4), other scheduling policies via the same formulation (p. 46).

method_links.note: A probability question (the overflow exponent) written as an optimization problem whose value is the answer and whose optimal solution gives the structure (most likely modes); convexity reduces it to finite-dimensional programs; the class is convex rate-function minimization, not LP, conic or MIO; close to SW2.

Policy families indexed by one knob (GPS weight phi1, GLQF slope theta); the curve of class-wise exponents is published and dominance proved for every admissible input; the bad case (fairness, delay) is named but not modelled.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The large-buffer exponent ranks the scheduling policies.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: rare-event exponent as an optimal-control value
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lower bound from the best scenario, a matching upper bound, and the optimal trajectory read as the dominant failure mode, used for admission control.

transferable: Compute a large-deviations exponent as the value of a deterministic control problem (scaled state, empirical rates as controls, integrated rate functions as cost, free horizon), with the policy only in the dynamics (pp. 16-18).
Simplify such problems with Jensen's inequality (constant controls per region) and time-scaling homogeneity, so optimal paths come from a short list of piecewise-linear shapes (pp. 18-20).
Use the optimal trajectory as the dominant failure scenario in design, e.g. admission control that claims the multiplexing gain worst-case rules forgo (p. 25).
Compare two parametric policy families by their curves of exponent pairs, then prove dominance for every admissible input process, not only the plotted one (pp. 40-44).
coauthors: Ioannis Ch. Paschalidis, John N. Tsitsiklis

quotes.text: This optimal control formulation is general enough to include any scheduling policy; only the dynamics of the system are policy dependent.
We argue that GLQF is preferable, at least in the absence of fairness considerations.

title: Rounding algorithms for covering problems
contribution: Two generic LP-rounding schemes for covering integer programs, randomized rounding with a nonlinear function (with derandomization) and deterministic dual-based rounding, that recover or match known bounds for set cover, general covering and facility location, yield an LP-free O(n^2) algorithm, and connect cut covering to random-graph thresholds through a conjecture.
problem_entry: IO (LO as the engine): hardness results give a 'unifying picture' but approximation algorithms are problem-specific and insights rarely transfer (pp. 1-2); two questions: why some problems approximate better, and whether good algorithms can be generated systematically (p. 2); class: covering IPs min cx, Ax >= b with nonnegative integer data, x 0-1 or integer (p. 2).
key_idea: Round the LP relaxation: randomized with P{x_j = 1} = 1 - (1 - x*_j)^k plus derandomization (set cover O(log m), general covering O(a_max log m), facility location O(log n) from the standard strong formulation with correlated rounding) (pp. 3-14); threshold rounding at 1/f gives the row-sum bound f for all covering problems (pp. 8-9); dual-based rounding (x_j = ceil(x*_j) on tight dual constraints) gives f + 1 and, with a structured optimal dual, f, and run in reverse an LP-free O(n^2) algorithm (pp. 14-22); cut covering linked to random-graph thresholds (Conjecture 1, pp. 24-25).
assumptions: Nonnegative integer A, b, c; a_ij <= b_i without loss (pp. 2, 7); bounds in m, n, D (max column sum), f (max row sum) and a_max (pp. 4, 8-10); cut covering with a set function f, where arbitrary f gives an Omega(n) LP gap even with 0-1 values (pp. 22-23).
proof_devices: Positive correlation of covering events: P(all satisfied) >= product of P(each satisfied) (p. 5)
Conditional expected cost bounded by k Z_LP/(1 - e^-k)^D, k chosen to balance; k = log D gives Theorem 1 (pp. 5-6)
Derandomization by a potential (cost + M times violated rows) with M from a small optimization and the method of conditional expectations (pp. 6-7, 13-14)
Chernoff-type lower-tail bound for independent non-identical variables (Proposition 1, pp. 9-10)
Threshold-rounding feasibility by contradiction with LP feasibility (Theorem 2, pp. 8-9)
Complementary-slackness bound for dual rounding (Theorem 5, p. 15); a 'reduction' moving any optimal dual to a structured one in at most min(m, n) steps (Proposition 2, Theorem 6, pp. 16-19)
Omega(n) integrality-gap example for arbitrary f (pp. 22-23)
positioning: Builds on Raghavan-Thompson's linear rounding and Goemans-Williamson's nonlinear MAXSAT rounding (pp. 2-4) and on Hochbaum's and Hall-Hochbaum's dual heuristics (pp. 8, 14, 20); concedes Dobson's stronger column-sum bound (p. 11); reads the cut-covering primal-dual results as instances of its dual heuristic (p. 23); uses Alon's random-graph result (pp. 24-25).
writing: 'In our opinion' framing and four design questions (pp. 2, 4); headline 'the best possible approximation bounds for all these problems' (p. 2) against 'best known bounds for several covering problems' in the conclusion (p. 25) and a conceded weaker bound (p. 11); closing belief labelled 'not a formal mathematical statement' (p. 26).
limits_future: Dual heuristic gives no better guarantee and is 'considerably more complicated' (p. 20); no systematic way to choose the rounding function, a calculus-of-variations problem (p. 26); the randomized general-covering bound is weaker than Dobson's (p. 11); Conjecture 1 proved only for f = 1 (p. 24); future: which min-sum problems admit O(log n), the best rounding function, Conjecture 1 (p. 26).

transferable: Nonlinear randomized rounding for covering: round x_j up with probability 1 - (1 - x*_j)^k, bound the expected cost given feasibility using positive correlation of covering events, then derandomize with a penalty potential and conditional expectations (pp. 4-7).
For linking constraints such as x_ij <= y_j, round the parent variable first and the child conditionally, so the constraint holds surely (p. 12).
Threshold rounding at 1/f, with f the maximum row sum, gives a feasible cover within f of the LP (pp. 8-9).

In a primal-dual analysis, first transform an arbitrary optimal dual into one with the structure the proof needs; running the transformation in reverse can give an LP-free combinatorial algorithm (pp. 16-22).

quotes.text: The importance of the dual heuristic lies not so much in the guarantee it produces but rather in its proof.

Although this is not a formal mathematical statement we do not know of any example of a min-sum problem with a logarithmic or a sublogarithmic guarantee that cannot be formulated as a covering problem.
